red.focus: Reason from events to consequences without assuming cause
red.summary: Lawyers must distinguish an event happening before another from an event producing it. Learn a simple counterfactual question while recognizing its limits.
checklist: I can explain why sequence does not prove cause
I can ask what would happen without the alleged act
I can identify alternative causes worth investigating

sections.title: Before Is Not Because
sections.body_md: A patient takes a medicine and develops a rash the next day. The timing may raise a question, but does not establish cause. Other medicines, illness, allergies, or unrelated events could contribute. Legal reasoning begins by identifying the alleged causal link and asking what evidence supports it. A timeline is useful, but it is not a conclusion. This is why a lawyer should carefully distinguish a suspicious sequence from the factual connection a legal claim requires.

sections.title: The Counterfactual Question
sections.body_md: Imagine a driver runs a red light and collides with another car. Ask whether the crash would likely have happened without the violation. This is a simple counterfactual: compare the actual world with a carefully defined alternative. The question can clarify ordinary causation, but the result depends on reliable evidence about movement, timing, and other drivers. The legal system may also ask whether the kind of injury falls within the scope of the rule.

sections.title: Investigate Other Causes
sections.body_md: A building collapse may involve weak construction, an earthquake and poor maintenance. A useful analysis identifies each candidate cause instead of choosing the most dramatic. Evidence can include engineering reports, inspection records and witness accounts. Different legal tests may handle multiple contributors in different ways. The first skill is humility: say which link is established, which remains only plausible, and which fact would help distinguish the alternatives.

yellow.focus: Separate factual causation from scope of legal responsibility
yellow.summary: Use counterfactual reasoning carefully while identifying the distinct legal limits on attributing consequences. Learn why proving a physical chain does not automatically establish liability.
checklist: I can analyze a simple but-for inquiry
I can distinguish causation from remoteness or scope

sections.title: What Would Have Happened Otherwise?
sections.body_md: A contractor fails to secure scaffolding, and it falls during ordinary winds. The factual question is whether the injury would have occurred without that failure. Evidence about wind speed, securing methods and the structure matters. A but-for question is useful here, but not sufficient for every kind of case. If several independent negligent actions were each sufficient, a simplistic counterfactual test might yield a misleading answer. Courts and legislation may provide special approaches.

If several independent negligent actions were each sufficient, a simplistic counterfactual test might yield a misleading answer. Courts and legislation may provide special approaches.

sections.title: Causation and Scope Are Separate
sections.body_md: Even a proven physical connection may not lead to liability for every later consequence. A legal rule can limit responsibility to particular kinds of harm, protected interests or foreseeable consequences. Different jurisdictions describe this through remoteness, proximate cause, scope of duty, or other standards. A careful lawyer applies the relevant legal doctrine rather than treating factual science as a complete answer to legal responsibility. The point is to avoid hiding normative judgments inside the word cause.

sections.title: Show Each Link in the Argument
sections.body_md: An effective causation paragraph states the alleged conduct, outcome, evidence connecting them, and the most plausible alternative explanation. It then applies any distinct legal-scope requirement. If a step is uncertain, say so and identify the evidence required. This structure makes the logic inspectable by the client and court. A confident conclusion without its causal links may sound persuasive but gives the reader no reason to trust it.

orange.focus: Compare competing causal explanations under uncertainty
orange.summary: Analyze statistical and testimonial proof without confusing association with individual causation. Use probability responsibly within the tribunal's evidentiary standard.
checklist: I can distinguish association from causation
I can analyze bias and confounding in causal evidence
I can explain the legal role of expert testimony

sections.title: Association Is a Starting Point
sections.body_md: A study finds that workers at a plant have higher rates of a disease. That association may suggest exposure matters, but other variables such as age, smoking, work history, and measurement quality could explain part of the pattern. Causal research tests whether the relationship persists under suitable controls. A legal analyst should ask what exposure was measured, how outcomes were defined, and whether the study supports general or individual causation. Statistics do not relieve counsel of those questions.

sections.title: Experts Do Not Decide the Law
sections.body_md: An expert can explain scientific methods and likely causal mechanisms, while the legal decision maker applies the evidentiary burden and substantive rules. The court may test expert reliability, qualifications and relevance under jurisdiction-specific standards. A lawyer who quotes an expert's probability without explaining what it measures can mislead the reader. The careful approach separates the expert's inference, its uncertainty, the facts particular to the claimant, and the legal conclusion drawn from all admissible evidence.

sections.title: Reason Through Alternatives
sections.body_md: Suppose multiple possible exposures might explain an injury. List them, identify what each predicts, and ask which records could distinguish them. A strong argument does not need to pretend alternative causes are impossible. It shows why the total evidence satisfies or fails to satisfy the applicable standard despite those alternatives. Where proof remains incomplete, report the uncertainty in ordinary language. Such candor is especially important when a client's health or livelihood depends on the conclusion.

black.focus: Defend legal causal reasoning under multiple uncertainties
black.summary: At doctoral depth, address causal overdetermination, complex systems, and the costs of evidentiary error. Build an argument that distinguishes scientific uncertainty from the policy choice of allocating risk.
checklist: I can critique overly simple counterfactual tests
I can identify the trade-off in evidence standards
I can propose a principled approach to diffuse causation

sections.title: No Single Test Solves Every Case
sections.body_md: Multiple sufficient causes, cumulative exposure and feedback-driven systems can break the intuition that each event must be necessary for an outcome. Legal doctrines sometimes adapt causation through special tests, presumptions or statutory allocation rules. A doctoral lawyer must identify precisely where a traditional test fails before proposing another. The choice changes who bears responsibility and who receives relief, so it requires both analytic discipline and legitimate institutional authority.

sections.title: Uncertainty Has Unequal Consequences
sections.body_md: A demanding causal threshold may deny redress to victims of diffuse industrial harm. A very permissive rule may assign liability to actors who did not cause the particular injury. These errors have moral, economic and institutional costs. A scholarly analysis should model available evidence, explain the false-positive and false-negative risks, and identify who can best produce missing information. The resulting rule cannot be justified by a single sympathetic example; it must be defensible across a class of cases.

sections.title: A Responsible Reform Argument
sections.body_md: Consider pollution from many facilities along a river. One proposal might rely on individual proof for damages while requiring preventive monitoring or risk reduction under a separate regulatory standard. Another might create a carefully bounded compensation fund. Each needs a legal source, transparent eligibility, appeals and finance. A good doctoral argument distinguishes the factual science from a chosen policy response and explains why the response protects affected people without making blame arbitrary.
